summary: Describes the structure, content, construction and meaning of language tags, used to say what language an object is in. It also covers registering values for them and creating private-use extensions. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5646 defines language tags such as en-US and explains how to build and interpret them. The tag's parts can identify a language, writing system, region, or other registered distinction.

questions: what is the iana language subtag registry
subtitle: A common format for identifying the language and writing conventions of content.

tldr.problem: Applications need a consistent way to identify the language and relevant written form of information.
tldr.mechanism: A language tag combines registered subtags for language, script, region, variants, extensions, or private use; IANA maintains the subtag registry.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5646 defines the BCP 47 language-tag format and registry process, and obsoletes RFC 4646.

today: RFC 5646 is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 4646. It defines language-tag structure and the registry process used by BCP 47.

sections.title: Why Language Tags Are Used
sections.content:
A language tag labels the language used in information or the language a user prefers. Software can use that information to select or process content, such as choosing a page, dictionary, speech voice, or rendering method.

RFC 5646 is one part of BCP 47. Together with RFC 4647, it defines how language tags are formed and matched.
sections.plainLanguage: A language tag tells software what language a piece of content uses. This helps programs choose and handle information that people can understand.

sections.title: The Parts of a Language Tag
sections.content:
A tag is a sequence of alphanumeric subtags separated by hyphens. It can include a primary language, an optional script and region, variants, registered extensions, and optional private-use subtags.

Each subtag has a defined position and syntax. Tags are case-insensitive; capitalization is a formatting convention and does not change meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: A language tag is built from short parts separated by hyphens. Letter case does not change what the tag means.

sections.title: What the Subtags Identify
sections.content:
The primary language subtag names a language. A script subtag identifies a writing system, and a region subtag can identify a regional variety or usage. Variant subtags identify other recognized distinctions.

Extensions add application-defined information while retaining a language tag. A private-use sequence begins with x and has meaning only by private agreement. The IANA Language Subtag Registry records valid registered subtags and their descriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The first part identifies a language, and later parts can add useful details such as script or region. Parts marked for private use only make sense to people who share the relevant agreement.

sections.title: Choosing and Processing Tags
sections.content:
Choose a tag that is as precise as the content requires, but do not add details that do not help distinguish it. Use registry guidance such as Prefix and Suppress-Script, and prefer a registered Preferred-Value when one is defined.

Tags are well-formed when they match the syntax. A tag is valid only when its relevant subtags are registered, or it is a grandfathered tag, and it has no repeated variant or extension singleton.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the shortest tag that gives the distinctions the application needs. A tag can follow the syntax and still be invalid if its registered parts do not meet the rules.

sections.title: Maintaining the Subtag Registry
sections.content:
The IANA Language Subtag Registry is a machine-readable list of registered subtags and tags. Its records have defined fields, and changes follow a public registration process overseen by a Language Subtag Reviewer.

Registry rules preserve the meaning and validity of existing tags over time. Extension identifiers are tracked separately in the Language Tag Extensions Registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry is the shared source for registered language-tag parts. A review process controls changes so that tags already in use keep their meaning.

sections.title: Security and Data Handling
sections.content:
Language tags can reveal information that may help infer a sender's nationality. A tag does not guarantee that text contains only characters from the named language or script.

Tags can grow without a fixed maximum because variants, extensions, and private-use parts can be added. Implementations need to guard against buffer overflows and should avoid cutting a tag in a way that changes its meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: A language tag may disclose information about its sender, and it does not prove which characters appear in the content. Software must also handle long tags safely.
